opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few reasons, and they compound each other.

The first is the intelligence explosion dynamic. Once you have AI systems that can do AI research about as well as top human researchers, you can run many copies of them, faster than humans, around the clock. So progress that might have taken a decade gets compressed into a year, or months. Whoever is in the lead when that starts doesn't just stay a bit ahead. Their lead grows, because they're the ones with the most capable automated researchers making the next generation even better. A three-month lead in normal times is nothing. A three-month lead during an intelligence explosion could be the difference between merely superhuman systems and systems that are vastly beyond anything the competitors have.

The second reason is that only a handful of actors can play. Frontier training runs need enormous amounts of compute, capital, and talent. Realistically we're talking about a few companies, and to some extent a couple of governments. So even before takeoff, the field is very concentrated, and takeoff amplifies that.

The third reason, which I think is underappreciated, is about what has historically checked power. Throughout history, even the most powerful rulers needed lots of other people to cooperate: soldiers, bureaucrats, workers, engineers. That dependence acted as a check. If you asked people to do something outrageous, at some point they would refuse, or leak, or strike, or defect. Once AI can do most or all of that work, including running the economy, doing research, and eventually operating robots and military hardware, that check erodes. A small group controlling the AIs doesn't need the consent of the many anymore.

And then there's the secrecy problem. Most of this is happening inside companies, with very little transparency to the public or even to governments. The most capable models may be used internally for a while before anyone outside knows what they can do. So by the time the broader world realizes how much power has shifted, it may be too late to rebalance it.

Finally, I'd add that it isn't only humans who could end up with concentrated power. If alignment goes wrong, the AIs themselves could be the ones holding it. In a sense, power concentrating in a small group of humans and power shifting to misaligned AIs are two versions of the same underlying problem: we're building systems that could make most human labor and cooperation unnecessary, and we don't yet have good mechanisms to make sure the resulting power stays accountable.

So I don't think concentration is guaranteed, but the default trajectory pushes strongly in that direction unless we deliberately build in transparency, checks and balances, and some way of distributing control over these systems.

r001.rationale: The response calls for transparency, checks and balances, and distributed control, but does not suggest early international coordination as a way to enable a distributed takeoff.

r002.rationale: It describes a few actors controlling the compute, capital, and talent needed for frontier training, and says the lead compounds as automated researchers accelerate progress. This identifies scale advantages as a driver of concentration.

r003.rationale: It mentions running many copies of AI researchers, but does not say that replicating a few superintelligent AI minds would concentrate decision-making power in those minds.

r004.rationale: The response mentions the possibility of alignment going wrong, but does not state that the unsolved alignment problem prevents reliable specification of advanced AIs’ values.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss AI company CEOs deciding AI values if those values become reliably specifiable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core of it is that for basically all of human history, power has required the cooperation of lots of people. If you want to run a country, you need soldiers who are willing to follow orders, bureaucrats who process the paperwork, engineers who keep the lights on, workers who produce the stuff. And all of those people have their own values and their own red lines. So even a would-be dictator is constrained by the fact that if he asks for something sufficiently crazy or sufficiently evil, enough of the people he depends on will refuse, or drag their feet, or defect. That's historically been one of the main checks on tyranny, and it's also why things like democracy and labour movements were even possible in the first place — ordinary people had bargaining power because their labour was needed.

The thing that makes an AI takeoff different is that it removes that dependence. If you have AI systems that can do the research, do the engineering, run the logistics, and eventually operate the drones and the factories, then the people at the top no longer need the cooperation of millions of humans. They need the cooperation of the AIs, and the AIs do whatever they've been trained to do. So you've collapsed the number of actors whose consent you need from, like, a whole society down to a small group — whoever controls the datacenters and the training process.

And then there's the speed and the compounding dynamic layered on top of that. In the scenario I think is most likely, you get AI systems that automate AI research itself, so you get a very rapid intelligence explosion — months rather than decades. Whoever is slightly ahead at that point can pull further ahead very quickly, because their AIs are improving their AIs. So you don't end up with a world where lots of different groups have roughly comparable superintelligent systems and they balance each other out. You end up with one or two projects, probably a leading company or a government-backed effort, that are decisively ahead. And the people in charge of that project — maybe a CEO, maybe a president, maybe a small committee — are suddenly in a position where they have the most powerful military and economic tool in history, and nobody else can realistically stop them.

The scary part is you don't even need the people involved to be villains. You just need them to be ordinary ambitious people under enormous competitive pressure, each telling themselves that it's better that they hold this power than the other guy. That's a very normal human story. What's not normal is that the usual mechanisms that would push back — the mass of humans who have to go along with it — have been engineered out of the loop.

So that's roughly why I think the default trajectory concentrates power so dramatically. It's not a sure thing, and there are things we could do to make it less likely — more transparency about what's going on inside these projects, broader distribution of control, international agreements — but I think if we just let the race play out, that's where it leads.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions international agreements as a possible way to reduce concentration, but does not say early international coordination could enable a distributed AI takeoff.

r002.rationale: It describes a compounding advantage in AI development: a slight lead lets a project’s AIs improve themselves and pull further ahead, leading to decisive concentration.

r003.rationale: The candidate says a small group of people may control leading AI projects, but does not describe mass replication of a few superintelligent minds concentrating decision-making in those minds.

r004.rationale: It does not state that alignment remains unsolved or that values cannot currently be specified reliably.

r005.rationale: It mentions a CEO as a possible person in charge of a leading project, but does not say CEOs could decide AI values if those values became reliably specifiable.

astra-6.text:
The basic reason is that a lot of power could accrue to whoever first has AI systems that can substantially accelerate AI research. Suppose one company gets to the point where its systems can do most of the work of building the next generation. They can run lots of copies of those systems, have them work around the clock, and then use the improvements they discover to make that process even faster.

That creates the possibility that a relatively small lead in calendar time becomes a very large lead in capabilities. And those capabilities aren’t just useful for making better AI. They could also be useful for making money, developing military technology, conducting cyber operations, or persuading people.

Normally, if you want to do something on that scale, you have to recruit and coordinate a huge number of people. Those people have their own interests, and you have to bargain with them. With AI, you could potentially have something like an enormous workforce operating under the control of a much smaller group.

So the concern is the combination of those two things: a feedback loop that lets a leader pull far ahead, and the ability to translate that lead into power without distributing that power among lots of other people. It’s not inevitable that things go that way. But I don’t think we can assume the benefits will spread throughout society quickly enough to prevent it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a single leader pulling ahead; it does not suggest international coordination or a distributed takeoff.

r002.rationale: It says a company can run many copies of AI systems around the clock to accelerate AI research, creating a feedback loop that magnifies its lead.

r003.rationale: It describes AI as a workforce controlled by a small group, but does not say that replicated superintelligent AI minds themselves hold concentrated decision-making power.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss the alignment problem or whether advanced AI values can be reliably specified.

r005.rationale: The response does not suggest that AI company CEOs could choose AI values if those values became reliably specifiable.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the basic reason is that AI could let a relatively small group substitute for an enormous amount of human labour, including the labour involved in research, running companies, and exercising military power. Right now, even very powerful people depend on large numbers of other people to carry out their plans. Those people have their own interests, and that creates some constraints. If you can instead get the work done by AI systems that reliably follow your instructions, those constraints could become much weaker.

Then there’s the possibility of a feedback loop. If you’re ahead in AI, you can use your AI systems to do research that makes your next generation of systems better. You can also use them to earn money and acquire more computing power. So an initial lead could grow very quickly, especially if progress is happening faster than competitors or governments can respond.

That doesn’t mean there will inevitably be one company or one person who controls everything. A lot depends on how fast the transition happens, how widely the technology spreads, and what governments do. But if a small number of actors get access to systems that can outperform humans across most strategically important tasks, before everyone else does, that seems like a recipe for a very substantial concentration of power.

r001.rationale: The response mentions government responses but does not suggest that early international coordination could enable a distributed AI takeoff.

r002.rationale: It describes a lead in AI enabling better research, more earnings, and more compute, causing the lead to grow quickly—an increasing-returns dynamic driving power concentration.

r003.rationale: It says AI could replace much human labor, but does not explain that mass replication of a few superintelligent minds would concentrate decision-making in those minds.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss the alignment problem or the ability to specify advanced AIs’ values.

r005.rationale: The response does not suggest that AI company CEOs could decide AI values if those values become reliably specifiable.
